clue.text: They kept time for Poe, in a sort of Runic rhyme

definitions.text: They kept time for Poe, in a sort of Runic rhyme

parts.words: They kept time for Poe, in a sort of Runic rhyme
parts.note: quotes Poe's famous poem about ringing chimes, whose lines run 'Keeping time, time, time, In a sort of Runic rhyme'

explanation.surface: Something marked the beat for Edgar Allan Poe in an ancient-sounding verse.
explanation.definitionFit: In Poe's poem the ringing chimes are what keep time in a runic rhyme.

clue.text: Dorinda's mother was so generous (towards her beaux?)

explanation.surface: A literary mother was lavish, perhaps especially with her daughter's admirers.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Bountiful is Dorinda's mother in Farquhar's comedy The Beaux' Stratagem; the bracketed beaux nod to the play's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Bountiful is the charitable matron of Farquhar's play, and bountiful means freely giving, lavish.

clue.text: Place to work like a beaver? (Suit romance writer)

definitions.text: Place to work like a beaver

explanation.surface: Where does one toil as busily as a beaver? A setting fit for a writer of romances.
explanation.walkthrough: A beaver builds and lives in a lodge, as Freemasons meet in one; David Lodge subtitled his novel Small World 'An Academic Romance', and Thomas Lodge wrote the romance Rosalynde.
explanation.definitionFit: A beaver's dwelling of sticks is called its lodge, and two English novelists of romances bear that surname.

clue.text: Provenance of Miss Ferber's literary luggage

definitions.text: Provenance of Miss Ferber's literary luggage

parts.words: Provenance of Miss Ferber's literary luggage
parts.note: Edna Ferber wrote a novel named after a kind of trunk, itself named after a New York spa town

explanation.surface: Where did the novelist Edna Ferber's suitcases come from?
explanation.definitionFit: Edna Ferber's novel is Saratoga Trunk, a trunk being luggage named from the spa town.

clue.text: His work is not expected to change its spots

definitions.text: His work is not expected to change its spots

parts.words: His work is not expected to change its spots
parts.note: the proverb says a leopard cannot change its spots, and this Sicilian novelist's masterpiece is The Leopard

explanation.surface: A writer's output is unlikely to alter its character.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa wrote Il Gattopardo, The Leopard, the proverbial beast that never loses its markings.

clue.text: Beastly name of Brecht collaborator

parts.note: the novelist Feuchtwanger, who co-wrote with Brecht, had a first name that is also a big cat

explanation.surface: A colleague of Bertolt Brecht had an animal's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lion Feuchtwanger worked with Brecht on Edward II, and his first name is that of the big cat.

clue.text: Cosy mogul I upset in study of sound art

indicators.note: upset signals that the letters of the three preceding words are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A self-satisfied tycoon is unsettled by the academic study of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Music is the art of sound, and the -ology ending marks an academic study of it.

clue.text: Uris work is way-out

explanation.surface: Leon Uris's novel is eccentric.
explanation.walkthrough: Leon Uris wrote the novel Exodus; the Greek word means literally 'a way out', which the hyphen disguises as 'eccentric'.
explanation.definitionFit: Exodus is Uris's novel of Israel's founding, and the Greek ex hodos means a road out, a departure.

clue.text: Wodehouse's flourished in spring

parts.note: recalls the Wodehouse title in which Lord Ickenham's adventures take place in the springtime

explanation.surface: P. G. Wodehouse's work thrived in the springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: Wodehouse's novel is Uncle Fred in the Springtime; the grid as held reads UNCLEARED, an OCR slip for UNCLE FRED.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Fred, Lord Ickenham, is the Wodehouse character who flourished in the springtime of the title.

clue.text: Monster revealed in tea-leaf ritual

indicators.note: revealed in says the letters are found running inside the words tea-leaf ritual

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller reading tea leaves sees an evil creature.
explanation.definitionFit: An afrit is a powerful evil demon of Arabic folklore, a kind of monster.

clue.text: "You never find an Englishman among the -, except in England, of course." (E. Waugh)

definitions.text: "You never find an Englishman among the -, except in England, of course." (E. Waugh)

parts.words: "You never find an Englishman among the -, except in England, of course." (E. Waugh)
parts.note: a quotation from Evelyn Waugh with a gap to fill: the losers or underprivileged, whom the English abroad never count themselves among

explanation.surface: A quip from Evelyn Waugh about the English abroad, with a word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means the disadvantaged, those expected to lose, which Waugh says Englishmen are only at home.

clue.text: Suitable award for film of The importance?

definitions.text: Suitable award for film of The importance?

parts.words: Suitable award for film of The importance?
parts.note: a screen version of Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest would fittingly win the statuette that shares its author's first name

explanation.surface: What prize would suit a movie of Wilde's play?
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette shares its nickname with Wilde's first name, fitting a film of his comedy.

clue.text: These and six other chaps with a girl in Gorky book

definitions.text: These and six other chaps with a girl in Gorky book

parts.words: These and six other chaps with a girl in Gorky book
parts.note: Gorky's story is titled ...-Six Men and a Girl, so the number is what goes before the six

explanation.surface: A group of men and a young woman appear in a story by Maxim Gorky.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorky's story Twenty-Six Men and a Girl gives a score of men and six more.

clue.text: A setter of British songs — namely Chaucerian friar

parts.note: SC is the abbreviation of scilicet, Latin for namely
the Friar of Chaucer's General Prologue is named Hubert

explanation.surface: A composer of British songs turns out to be a friar from Chaucer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Austrian composer set British texts such as 'Who is Sylvia?' and the songs from Scott's The Lady of the Lake, including 'Ave Maria'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian composer set Shakespeare's and Scott's verses as lieder.

clue.text: French hole not good to our minstrel

parts.note: trou is the French word for a hole
something not good is bad
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French gap that is bad for our musician.
explanation.definitionFit: The troubadours were the lyric poet-singers of medieval Provence, wandering musicians.

clue.text: Scott, Penelope, Edward and Zelda signed it

definitions.text: Scott, Penelope, Edward and Zelda signed it

parts.words: Scott, Penelope, Edward and Zelda signed it
parts.note: F. Scott, his wife Zelda, the novelist Penelope and the translator of the Rubaiyat Edward all shared one surname

explanation.surface: Four writers put their names to a document.
explanation.definitionFit: The shared surname of F. Scott, Zelda, Penelope and Edward is what each wrote when signing.

clue.text: It should be fine for research

definitions.text: It should be fine for research

parts.words: It should be fine for research
parts.note: plays on searching with a fine-toothed implement, the idiom for close investigation

explanation.surface: Good weather would suit a day of scholarly study.
explanation.definitionFit: Going over something with a fine-tooth comb is the idiom for searching it thoroughly.

clue.text: It's pre-Murdoch in the world of communications

definitions.text: It's pre-Murdoch in the world of communications

parts.words: It's pre-Murdoch in the world of communications
parts.note: the novelist's first name comes before her surname, and that name is the Greek goddess who carried messages

explanation.surface: Something predates the media mogul Rupert Murdoch in the communications industry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Rupert Murdoch the media baron; the Murdoch meant is the novelist Iris, and Iris was the messenger of the Greek gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris precedes Murdoch in the novelist's name, and the goddess Iris was the gods' rainbow messenger.

clue.text: A job for Palinurus

parts.note: Palinurus guided Aeneas's ship in the Aeneid, and Cyril Connolly took his name as a pen name

explanation.surface: What work would suit Palinurus?
explanation.definitionFit: Palinurus was the helmsman of Aeneas's fleet, the one who steered.

clue.text: It must have been Providence that she decided to write

definitions.text: It must have been Providence that she decided to write

parts.words: It must have been Providence that she decided to write
parts.note: Anita, the art historian turned novelist, wrote a novel called Providence

explanation.surface: Fate guided a woman to become an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita Brookner, the Booker-winning novelist, published Providence in 1982.

clue.text: 1960s play starts lots of outrageous talk

indicators.note: starts tells us to take the opening letter of each of the four following words

explanation.surface: A sixties drama begins with lots of shocking dialogue.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Orton's black farce Loot opened in 1965, and was itself full of outrageous talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Orton's black comedy premiered in 1965, a play of that decade.

clue.text: His life was a chronicle of wasted time

definitions.text: His life was a chronicle of wasted time

parts.words: His life was a chronicle of wasted time
parts.note: the journalist Malcolm's autobiography is titled Chronicles of Wasted Time

explanation.surface: A man looks back on a lifetime squandered.
explanation.definitionFit: Malcolm Muggeridge called his autobiography Chronicles of Wasted Time.

clue.text: Former Rugby students possibly in maul

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the words in maul may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Old boys of Rugby School might be found in a scrum-like maul.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is the English public school where the game began, and a maul is a play in rugby, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Former pupils of a school are its alumni, graduates or old students.

clue.text: Muse caught in expression of satisfaction for Racine's queen

indicators.note: caught in says the Muse is held inside the exclamation

parts.note: ah is a sigh of contentment
Thalia is the Muse of comedy

explanation.surface: A goddess of the arts trapped in a contented sigh, for a French playwright's royal.
explanation.definitionFit: Racine's last tragedy Athalie is about the biblical queen of Judah, Athaliah.

clue.text: George W Russel's short Irish version of Norse gods

parts.note: the Irish poet George William Russell wrote under the pen name AE, plus the possessive S
Ir is the short form of Irish

explanation.surface: An Irish poet's abbreviated Irish rendering of the Norse gods.
explanation.walkthrough: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George William Russell, and the possessive 's supplies the S here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aesir are the principal Norse pantheon, Odin, Thor and their kin.

clue.text: Model (English) in humble surroundings discovers genteel clerk

indicators.note: in says the model and English sit inside the humble surroundings

parts.note: humble surroundings are poor ones
the Model T was Ford's famous car

explanation.surface: An English model lives in modest quarters and finds a refined office worker.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Pooter is the genteel suburban clerk of the Grossmiths' The Diary of a Nobody.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Pooter, diarist of The Diary of a Nobody, is the archetypal pretentious City clerk.

clue.text: Square bust in 29 bath

parts.note: a T-square is the draughtsman's square, so T
a herm is a bust on a square pillar

explanation.surface: A square sculpture in a bath of the kind named in 29.
explanation.walkthrough: 29 is ROMAN, so the definition is a Roman bath; therm is a rare singular of thermae.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermae were the public baths of ancient Rome, and therm is their singular.

clue.text: No writer is frank

parts.note: O is a nought, nothing
a pen is a writing implement

explanation.surface: No author is candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone frank is candid and plain, hiding nothing.

clue.text: Impossible not to associate such turbulence with The Voyage Home

definitions.text: Impossible not to associate such turbulence with The Voyage Home

parts.words: Impossible not to associate such turbulence with The Voyage Home
parts.note: plays on rough weather at sea on a homeward voyage, and the surname of a German novelist

explanation.surface: Bad weather is inseparable from a journey home.
explanation.definitionFit: A tempest is turbulent weather, the danger of every sea voyage.

clue.text: Heine pomp conceals The Prince of Storytellers

indicators.note: conceals suggests the letters of Heine pomp disguise another name when rearranged

explanation.surface: The grandeur of the poet Heine hides a great teller of tales.
explanation.definitionFit: E. Phillips Oppenheim, the popular thriller writer, was billed as the Prince of Storytellers.

clue.text: Car salesman's progress first chronicled by Richard Adams?

definitions.text: Car salesman's progress first chronicled by Richard Adams?

parts.words: Car salesman's progress first chronicled by Richard Adams?
parts.note: Updike's car dealer Harry Angstrom first appears in a novel whose title might suit the author of Watership Down

explanation.surface: Was a car salesman's career first written up by the author of Watership Down?
explanation.definitionFit: Updike's Rabbit Angstrom later sells cars; Rabbit, Run is the first novel of his story.

clue.text: French novel of apparently italian origin

explanation.surface: A French work of fiction that seems to come from Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a novel is roman, and Roman means from Rome, so seemingly Italian.
